hero.subtitle: If you were injured working in Oroville, workers' compensation may not be your only option. We can review your case at no cost and explain whether a third-party claim applies to what happened to you.

about.title: Oroville Workplace Injury Claims
about.longDescription: Work in Oroville looks different from one block to the next. Some people spend their shifts near the dam or along the Feather River, others move goods in and out of warehouses, staff medical offices, or drive routes that cross Oroville Dam Boulevard East and Olive Highway several times a day. When an injury happens on the clock, California workers' compensation is usually the only claim you can bring against your employer, and fault does not factor into it. That part is well known. What many Butte County workers do not hear is that a separate injury claim may exist when someone outside your employer contributed to the harm — a subcontractor on the same site, a property owner who ignored a hazard, the maker of a defective tool, or another driver on Feather River Boulevard. Oroville recorded 102 injury collisions in 2025, and some of those involved people who were simply working. We are here to help you understand both routes and explain what applies to your situation.

items.title: We look past the workers' comp ceiling
items.desc: Workers' compensation is usually the exclusive remedy against your employer in California, but it does not shield a negligent subcontractor, property owner, equipment maker, or other driver. We know how to identify a third party when one exists.

items.title: We help you stay inside the deadlines
items.desc: California expects you to report a work injury to your employer within 30 days, and a third-party injury claim generally must be filed within two years. Getting started early means those dates are tracked from the beginning.

items.title: No fee unless there is a recovery
items.desc: We work on contingency, and your initial consultation costs you nothing. Retaliation for reporting an injury is illegal in California, and we can address that too if it comes up.

items.question: I was hit by another driver while making deliveries on Olive Highway for my employer. Is that just a workers' comp case?
items.answer: Not necessarily. Because you were working, workers' compensation would typically cover your medical care and part of your lost wages. Since the other driver is a third party rather than your employer, you may also have a separate injury claim against that driver, and it carries California's two-year deadline. We can review both pieces together.

items.question: What if I waited a few weeks to report my injury?
items.answer: California asks you to report a work injury to your employer within 30 days, so a delay of a few weeks may still fall inside that window. Report it in writing as soon as you can and keep a copy. If your employer pushes back or treats you differently for reporting, that retaliation is illegal, and it is worth raising with us.

items.question: Can I be fired for filing a workplace injury claim in Butte County?
items.answer: No. California law prohibits employers from retaliating against workers who report an injury or file a workers' compensation claim. If you are demoted, cut from the schedule, or let go after reporting, tell us, because that conduct may support its own claim.
